steps.body: Every angle on the circle leans on Quadrant I. The **reference angle** is the acute angle between the terminal side and the X-AXIS — and the point at any angle has the SAME coordinates as its reference point, up to sign. Size from the reference, sign from the quadrant: that's the whole system.
Reference angles, on the circle itself.

widget.prompt: Rotate to 150°. Watch the coordinates, and notice which 30° angle it leans on.
widget.successFeedback: 150° sits in the second quadrant, and its reference angle is 30° — the acute angle back to the x-axis. That is why cos 150° = −cos 30° and sin 150° = +sin 30°: same size, signs set by the quadrant.
widget.lowFeedback: Not far enough round. 150° is past 90° but short of 180°.
widget.highFeedback: Too far round — you have passed 150°.

cml.actionGoal: Rotate to an angle and coordinate its quadrant, reference angle, point coordinates, sine, and cosine.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Keep the 30° reference angle but move the terminal side through all four quadrants. Which coordinate magnitudes stay the same, and which signs change?

explanation.prompt: How does the reference angle determine exact sine and cosine values at 150°?

options.label: The 30° reference triangle fixes the coordinate magnitudes, while quadrant II makes cosine negative and sine positive.
options.feedback: Exactly — reference angle supplies magnitude and quadrant supplies sign.

options.label: The reference angle makes both values identical to those at 30°, including their signs.
options.feedback: The magnitudes match, but the quadrant changes the sign of the horizontal coordinate.

explanationVariants: In Q3 the reference is θ − 180: 225 − 180 = 45°.

widget.prompt: What is the reference angle of 225°, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 135 is 360 − 225 — the Quadrant IV rule applied in Q3. Past 180°, measure FORWARD from it: 225 − 180 = 45°.
225° is the full angle — the reference is its acute distance to the x-axis: 45°.

steps.body: Three rules, one per outer quadrant — all measuring the gap to the nearest x-axis crossing. **Q2: 180 − θ. Q3: θ − 180. Q4: 360 − θ.** In radians the same shapes: π − θ, θ − π, 2π − θ. Locate the quadrant first; the rule follows.

widget.prompt: What is the reference angle of 300°, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 120 is 300 − 180 — the Q3 rule. 300° lives in Q4, measured back from the crossing at 360°: 360 − 300 = 60°.
300° sits 60° short of 360, not 30 — that would be 330°'s reference. Here: 60°.

explanationVariants: 5π/6 is in Q2, so the reference is π − 5π/6 = π/6: n = 6.
In degrees: 150° sits 30° from the axis, and 30° = π/6.

widget.prompt: The reference angle of 5π/6 is π/n. What is n?

commonErrors.feedback: π/3 is 60° — but 5π/6 = 150° sits only 30° = π/6 from the x-axis.
The 5 is the original numerator recycled — the reference is π − 5π/6 = π/6.

steps.body: Now compute anything: **magnitude from the reference angle, sign from A-S-T-C.** cos 150°: reference 30° gives magnitude cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.87; Quadrant II makes cosine negative. Answer: −0.87. Two lookups, one sign check — the whole circle from one quadrant's table.

commonErrors.feedback: The size is right but 150° is Quadrant II, where x < 0 — cosine comes out NEGATIVE: −0.87.
−0.5 borrows sin 30°'s magnitude — cos 150° takes COS of the reference: cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.87, negated.

explanationVariants: Reference: 225 − 180 = 45°; magnitude sin 45° = √2/2 ≈ 0.71; Q3 makes sine negative: −0.71.
Q3 is the T quadrant — sine AND cosine both flip negative there.

commonErrors.feedback: Magnitude right, sign missed — 225° is Q3, below the x-axis, so sine is NEGATIVE: −0.71.
−0.5 borrows the 30° family — but 225°'s reference is 45°, whose sine is √2/2 ≈ 0.71. Answer −0.71.

hints: Locate the quadrant (225° → Q3) and its rule: θ − 180.
Q3 is below the x-axis — apply the sign.

takeaways: Reference angle: the acute gap to the X-axis — never the y-axis.
Q2: 180−θ · Q3: θ−180 · Q4: 360−θ (same shapes with π in radians).
Magnitude from the reference, sign from A-S-T-C.
steps.teaser: Next: the exact values themselves — the little table the special triangles hand you.

concept.body: One reference, slowly. 120° lands in Quadrant II, between 90° and 180°. Its terminal side is 60° short of the x-axis crossing at 180° — so the reference angle is 180 − 120 = 60°. Always measure to the x-axis, whichever crossing is nearer.

explanationVariants: The x-axis crossing at 180° is the near one; the gap to it is the reference.

widget.prompt: What is the reference angle of 120°, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 120° is the angle itself — the reference is its gap to the x-axis: 180 − 120 = 60°.
30° measures to the Y-axis at 90° — reference angles run to the X-axis: 60°.
